target.title: Lipreading using Convolutional Neural Network
target.version: Published proceedings version; no explicit version label on first page

read.pdf: Table 1 and Figs. 1–5 inspected, including plot graphics; references [1]–[22] read

entries.text: The authors present a CNN-based visual feature extraction approach as a novel visual speech recognition system.
entries.condition: The proposed system uses mouth-area images to predict phoneme posteriors for lipreading.

entries.text: The authors state that earlier CNN speech-recognition applications were limited to audio and that lipreading applications remained unaddressed.
entries.condition: This is the authors' novelty framing in the 2014 paper, not a current literature survey.
entries.quote: their applications towards lipreading remain unaddressed.

entries.text: The authors claim their approach avoids dedicated lip-shape models and hand-labeled training data.
entries.condition: Claim applies to the proposed bottom-up CNN visual feature extractor.

entries.text: The authors claim shift- and rotation-resistant image recognition and also describe some degree of shift, scale, and local-distortion invariance from shared weights.
entries.condition: Stated as a claimed CNN advantage; the paper does not separately test controlled shift or rotation robustness.
entries.quote: CNN guaran- tees shift- and rotation- resistant image recognition.

entries.text: The phoneme CNN has seven layers, four weighted layers, and approximately 1.19×10^5 parameters.
entries.condition: Three convolutional layers (C1, C3, C5) and one fully connected layer (F7); pooling layers are P2, P4, and P6.

entries.text: Table 1 gives a 1024-dimensional input, a 40-dimensional output, and layer sequence C1-P2-C3-P4-C5-P6-F7.
entries.condition: The output is a 40-way phoneme posterior distribution.

entries.text: CNN training maximizes multinomial logistic-regression likelihood, expressed as average correct-label log probability over training cases.
entries.condition: Supervised training uses phoneme labels as targets; specific optimizer settings and stopping rules are not reported.

entries.text: Training targets are 40 forced-aligned phoneme labels, including short pause; monophone HMMs trained with MFCCs and HTK/HVite provide the alignments.
entries.condition: One monophone HMM per phoneme is trained using audio MFCCs; HVite forced alignment assigns frame labels to mouth images.
entries.quote: and assigned 40 phoneme labels includ- ing short pause by conducting a forced alignment function of the HVite command of the HTK.

entries.text: The acoustic label-generation features are 39-dimensional MFCC features (13 coefficients plus first and second derivatives), sampled at 100 Hz.
entries.condition: Audio is 16 kHz, 16-bit, single-channel; video frames are resampled to match the number of MFCC frames.

entries.text: The dataset contains six male speakers and 300 Japanese words: 216 phonetically balanced training words and 84 important test words from ATR.
entries.unit: speakers; word types; training word types; test word types
entries.condition: The 216 phonetically balanced words and residual 84 words are the word-recognition train/test vocabulary split.

entries.text: Video is full-frontal 640×480, 8-bit monochrome, recorded at 100 Hz; audio is 16 kHz, 16-bit, single-channel.
entries.unit: pixels; bits; video Hz; audio samples/s; audio bits
entries.condition: Video frames are resampled to match MFCC frame count; the audio channel count is one.
entries.quote: Visual data was a full-frontal 640×480 pixels facial view with 8 bit monochrome, recorded at 100 Hz.

entries.text: Mouth regions are manually cropped to 128×128 pixels and resized to 32×32 pixels for visual-model training and evaluation.
entries.condition: The mouth crop is prepared from the original full-frontal visual data.
entries.quote: we pre- pared a trimmed dataset by manually cropping 128×128 pixels of mouth area from the original visual data and resizing them to 32×32 pixels.

entries.text: The phoneme experiment uses approximately 1.23×10^5 mouth-image samples; shuffled images are split 5/6 for training and 1/6 for evaluation.
entries.unit: image samples; training fraction; evaluation fraction
entries.condition: Images from six speakers and all 300 words are pooled before shuffling; the paper does not describe utterance- or session-grouped splitting.
entries.quote: The image data were shufﬂed and 5/6 of the data were used for training, while the rest was used for evaluation.

entries.text: The authors train an independent CNN for each speaker after a preliminary experiment found worse phoneme precision with one CNN across all speakers.
entries.condition: Each CNN is trained and evaluated on frames from its corresponding speaker; this is not a speaker-held-out protocol.
entries.quote: Therefore, we prepared an independent CNN for each speaker.

entries.text: Mean phoneme recognition rate is 58% across the 40 phonemes and six speakers.
entries.condition: Test portion is the remaining 1/6 of shuffled mouth-image samples from the same six speakers and all 300 words; one speaker-dependent CNN is used per speaker; no separate speaker-held-out set is used.
entries.quote: The average phoneme recognition performance for the 40 phonemes over six speakers is 58%.

entries.text: Reported mean per-phoneme recognition rates range from 60–100% for vowels and 20–80% for all other phonemes.
entries.condition: Ranges are reported across the vowel classes versus the other classes in the 40-phoneme, six-speaker experiment.

entries.text: The authors report that incorrectly recognized consonants are most often classified as vowels.
entries.condition: Qualitative observation from the 40-class phoneme confusion matrix over six speakers.

entries.text: The authors say consonant recognition, including visually explicit consonants, was below expectation and that phoneme target-labeling should be improved; consonants are shorter and have fewer training samples than vowels.
entries.condition: Authors attribute a direct effect on recognition to consonant label accuracy and the smaller number of consonant training samples.
entries.quote: To im- prove the recognition rate, the procedure to obtain phoneme target labels for CNN training should be improved.

entries.text: The authors attribute the single-CNN degradation mainly to limited variation in the prepared lip-region training images and say more images from different speakers are needed for speaker invariance.
entries.condition: This is the authors' explanation of the preliminary all-speaker CNN experiment, not a separately quantified analysis.
entries.quote: We think this degradation is mainly due to the limited variations of lip region images we prepared for the training of CNN.

entries.text: The current system uses speaker-dependent phoneme models and a common isolated-word model; the authors say the dataset is insufficient for a speaker-independent phoneme model across appearance variation.
entries.condition: No speaker-independent phoneme model is evaluated; the word-recognition model is described as common.

entries.text: The authors consider a speaker-independent CNN a future possibility, contingent on a larger dataset, more speakers, and artificial image deformation.
entries.condition: Prospective research direction; no speaker-independent result is presented.
entries.quote: by preparing a larger dataset, increasing the number of speakers, and applying artiﬁcial deformation for the image dataset.

entries.text: At inference, the CNN maps grayscale mouth images to phoneme posterior distributions, and the output time series serves as visual features for lipreading.
entries.condition: Posterior outputs are processed by a separate left-to-right GMM-HMM for isolated-word recognition.

entries.text: The CNN output is a 40-dimensional phoneme posterior sequence used as the visual feature representation.
entries.condition: Each time step corresponds to posterior probabilities over the 40 phoneme labels.
entries.quote: Estimated phoneme labels as visual features (40 dim)

entries.text: A left-to-right GMM-HMM performs isolated-word recognition over the CNN-derived visual feature sequences.
entries.condition: The paper identifies the decoder family and topology but does not provide full HMM/decoding settings.
entries.quote: Then, by processing the acquired visual feature sequences, left-to-right GMM-HMMs are utilized for isolated word recognition.

entries.text: The word decoder uses monophone HMMs with 8, 16, or 32 Gaussian-mixture components.
entries.condition: Each of the three mixture counts is crossed with three visual features (6×6, PCA, CNN), yielding nine models.
entries.quote: To recognize words from the phoneme label sequences generated by the CNN, mono- phone HMMs with 8, 16, and 32 GMM components are utilized.

entries.text: The word-recognition comparison uses 36-dimensional 6×6 rescaled images and 40-dimensional PCA features alongside the CNN features.
entries.condition: The two baselines are compared under the same three GMM component counts as the CNN feature condition.
entries.quote: One feature has 36 dimensions, generated by simply rescaling the images to 6×6 pixels, and the other feature has 40 dimensions, generated by compressing the raw images by PCA.

entries.text: For word-HMM training, CNN posterior features are generated from image sequences for the 216 training words.
entries.condition: These are the phonetically balanced word types; the separate test vocabulary contains the residual 84 words.

entries.text: Word recognition is evaluated on 84 test words from the same speaker, described as closed-speaker and open-vocabulary evaluation.
entries.condition: The 84 word types are held out from the word-HMM training vocabulary; evaluation is closed-speaker/open-vocabulary. The paper does not identify which speaker or state whether scores are pooled over all six speakers.
entries.quote: Evaluation is conducted with the 84 test words from the same speaker, yielding a closed-speaker and open-vocabulary eval- uation.

entries.text: CNN-derived features achieve higher word-recognition rates than both the 6×6-rescaling and PCA features; the Abstract characterizes this superiority as significant.
entries.condition: Nine models compare three feature types at 8, 16, and 32 GMM components on the 84 same-speaker, open-vocabulary test words.
entries.quote: These results demonstrate that the visual features acquired by the CNN attain higher word recognition capabilities than the other two.

entries.text: The highest plotted word-recognition rate is about 37%, at 32 GMM components for the CNN feature condition.
entries.condition: Figure 5 comparison: 84 test word types, same-speaker closed-speaker/open-vocabulary setting; CNN feature with 32 Gaussian components. The prose reports the maximum as about 37%.
entries.quote: The highest word recognition rate was about 37%

entries.text: The authors argue that visual inputs can be a reliable speech-recognition information source when visual feature extraction is appropriate.
entries.condition: The claim is based on the reported isolated-word experiment; no deployment or noisy-environment trial is reported.
entries.quote: this re- sult shows that visual inputs can be a reliable information source for a speech recognition task when a visual feature extraction mechanism is properly utilized.

entries.text: The authors interpret CNN posterior sequences as effective visual features for subsequent isolated-word recognition; the plotted analysis uses five representative Japanese vowels.
entries.condition: The first three principal components of the CNN posterior sequences are plotted for /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/, and /o/.

entries.text: The visual model is implemented with the open-source cuda-convnet software cited by the paper.
entries.condition: The paper cites Krizhevsky et al. [11] but does not link a repository; no repository-only conditions could be checked.

entries.text: The CNN experiment ran on a Core i7-3930K at 3.2 GHz with 6 cores, 32 GB RAM, and one GeForce GTX Titan with 6 GB onboard memory.
entries.unit: GHz; CPU cores; GB RAM; GPU count; GB GPU memory
entries.condition: Consumer-class personal computer; the paper does not give cuda-convnet version or code commit.

entries.text: The paper gives no random seeds, repeated-run count, or variation across independent training/evaluation runs.
entries.condition: Applies to the shuffled 5/6–1/6 phoneme-image split, CNN training, and word-recognition comparison.

entries.text: No validation split, model-selection criterion, early-stopping rule, or selection-data protocol is reported; architecture parameters are described only as empirically determined.
entries.condition: Applies to CNN structure/hyperparameter selection and to the choice among word-HMM component counts.

entries.text: Pixel-intensity normalization or standardization (such as mean subtraction or variance scaling) is not specified; only grayscale input, cropping, and resizing are described.
entries.condition: This concerns input-image normalization; the architecture does describe internal response-normalization layers.

entries.text: No chance-level or random-guess baseline is reported for either 40-class phoneme recognition or isolated-word recognition.
entries.condition: The paper reports recognition rates and feature baselines but does not calculate a chance baseline.

entries.text: No session-level or utterance-level partition is reported, and the paper does not say whether frames from one word recording can occur in both the training and evaluation subsets.
entries.condition: The stated split shuffles image samples; the paper identifies no session count or recording-group split.

entries.text: The paper does not state whether the 84 word-recognition test word images were excluded from the CNN's phoneme-model training; CNN training/evaluation is described over images from all 300 words.
entries.condition: The HMM vocabulary split is 216 training versus 84 test words, while the phoneme CNN image split is described separately over all 300 words.

entries.text: For word recognition, the paper does not identify the speaker(s), per-speaker test utterance counts, or whether the reported score pools or averages results across speakers.
entries.condition: The study dataset has six male speakers, but the evaluation text says only 'the same speaker' and the conclusion calls the isolated-word model common.
entries.quote: Evaluation is conducted with the 84 test words from the same speaker, yielding a closed-speaker and open-vocabulary eval- uation.

entries.text: No language model, pronunciation lexicon, decoding beam, or other use-time word-selection aid is specified; only a GMM-HMM decoder is described.
entries.condition: The paper does not state whether an external language model or lexicon participates in the isolated-word decision.

entries.text: HMM state counts, transition constraints beyond left-to-right topology, GMM covariance/initialization details, and decoding settings are not reported.
entries.condition: Only monophone HMMs and the 8/16/32 GMM-component settings are specified for the word experiment.

entries.text: No deployment, real-time, latency, environmental-robustness, or user-interaction evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: Evaluation is described as laboratory dataset experiments; there is no field or in-use trial.

entries.text: No statistical test, p-value, confidence interval, or repeated-run uncertainty is reported for the abstract's claim that CNN features significantly outperform the baselines.
entries.condition: Applies to the 84-word isolated-word comparison across 6×6, PCA, and CNN features with 8, 16, and 32 GMM components.
entries.quote: These results demonstrate that the visual features acquired by the CNN attain higher word recognition capabilities than the other two.

entries.text: The exact frame count and class/word distribution in the phoneme test subset are not reported; only the approximate full sample count and 1/6 evaluation fraction are given.
entries.condition: Applies to phoneme evaluation on the held-out shuffled image samples from the six speakers.

entries.text: No user-facing confirmation step or acceptance/rejection protocol is described.
entries.condition: The paper evaluates offline phoneme and isolated-word recognition rather than an interactive speech interface.

entries.text: No user correction, re-entry, or correction-learning process is described.
entries.condition: The system is evaluated as a visual recognition pipeline with no described post-recognition correction loop.

entries.text: The Abstract says CNN features significantly outperform dimensionality-compression features including PCA.
entries.condition: Isolated word recognition experiment; no test statistic is given (see t45).
entries.quote: The evaluation re- sults of our isolated word recognition experiment demonstrate that the visual features acquired by the CNN signiﬁcantly out- perform those acquired by conventional dimensionality com- pression approaches, including principal component analysis.

entries.text: Lip images are downsampled to 24x16 normalized pixel vectors (384 dimensions) as recognizer input.
entries.condition: gray-level lip region images, one male speaker
entries.quote: The resulting sequence of 384-dimensional “normalized pixel vectors” (one vector for each lip image frame) is then used as the input to the recognition algorithm.

entries.text: Recognition is performed by a modular multi-state time-delay neural network (MS-TDNN) with phoneme/viseme layers.
entries.condition: letter-sequence recognition
entries.quote: In the basic system a modular Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network (MS-TDNN) [5] is used to perform the recognition.

entries.text: Whole letter sequences are split 170 training, 15 cross-validation and 15 test; PCA and LDA statistics come from the training set only.
entries.condition: one male speaker, two sessions on the same day
entries.quote: 170 of the sequences were used as training data to set the weights of the network, 15 constituted the cross-validation set and 15 the test set.

entries.text: Tests use data from one male speaker.
entries.quote: We have tested the various recognizer versions on audiovisual speech data from one (male) speaker.

entries.text: ANN (MLP) outputs a posteriori phoneme probabilities per channel, fused and decoded with left-right phoneme HMMs.
entries.condition: video input is lip parameters from blue-ink chroma keying, not image pixels
entries.quote: this is achieved via the calculation of a joint a posteriori probability for each phoneme from the a posteriori probabilities of the audio and video channel.

entries.text: Video features are lip parameters obtained by chroma keying of lips coloured with blue ink.
entries.quote: the video features are extracted via a chroma key process, which requires coloring of the speakers lips with blue ink.

entries.text: Phonetic labels for ANN training come from audio recognition and forced Viterbi alignment.
entries.condition: automatic multi-stage labelling, no manual labelling

entries.text: The database is split into two subsets of similar size for training and final recognition.
entries.condition: utterance-level split
entries.quote: The database was subdivided into two subsets of similar size for training and ﬁnal recognition.

entries.text: Mouth ROIs are rescaled to 60x80 pixels and PCA-whitened to 32 dimensions before deep autoencoder feature learning.
entries.quote: Each mouth ROI was rescaled to 60 × 80 pixels and further reduced to 32 dimensions,6 using PCA whitening.

questions.q: What is the paper's component-level contribution?
questions.answer: A supervised CNN maps 32×32 mouth images to 40-way phoneme posteriors, which serve as visual features for a left-to-right GMM-HMM isolated-word recognizer.

questions.q: What does the reported 58% measure, and what is the evaluation split?
questions.answer: It is mean recognition rate over 40 phonemes and six speakers, evaluated on the remaining 1/6 of shuffled image samples with one speaker-dependent CNN per speaker; no speaker-held-out test is reported.

questions.q: What is the reported word-recognition result and comparison?
questions.answer: The best rate is about 37% for CNN features with 32 GMM components on 84 same-speaker, open-vocabulary test words; CNN features outperform the 6×6-rescaling and PCA baselines.

questions.q: Does the paper demonstrate speaker-independent recognition?
questions.answer: No. Phoneme models are speaker-dependent, the authors say the dataset is insufficient for a speaker-independent model, and a larger multi-speaker dataset with image deformation is left for future work.

questions.q: Which reproducibility and evaluation conditions remain unspecified?
questions.answer: Seeds and run counts, validation/selection data, pixel normalization, chance baselines, session/utterance grouping, possible overlap between CNN training and held-out word images, speaker-level aggregation, detailed HMM/LM decoding settings, and statistical significance tests are not reported.

questions.q: Triage: does Sec. 4 state that all 300 words trained the CNN?
questions.answer: Yes: "In the first (visual feature extraction) experiment, image sequences from all 300 words were used."
